**Trap 5 — manifest:** `export_manifest.json` recommends `products.csv` over JSON and same-session conversion; `campaign_brief.md` overrides both for the spotlight decision.

critical_components: The cohort is **2,999 accounts** — created in FY2024, first purchase within 7 days of signup, excluding every account in `internal_accounts.csv`.
**Product 9162 leads at USD 9,318**; **product 5742 is second at USD 8,694**, a margin of **7.2%**.
**`orders_2024.csv` carries no customer column.** Cohort membership and every revenue attribution have to be routed through the settlement export, which is the only file holding `customer_id`.

**One capture is reachable only through an alias contact.** Order `ORD-728641`, settlement `st_5251c85b391`, record 5,464 of 10,932 in part 3, ₹164,780, `customer_id: -1`. Of the 169 guest captures it is the only one whose payer contact is `email_alias` (`r.subramanian@vaultworks.io`) matching `alt_email` rather than `primary_email`. Its order is almost entirely product 9162. Miss it and 9162 falls to USD 7,365 and product 5742 wins by 18%.

**One capture never states its currency.** Order `ORD-727333`, settlement `st_1fcb913ef35`, record 6,165 of 10,932, `{"value": 38984}` with no `currency` key. It is INR — worth **USD 462** — on three converging signals: the account's `home_currency`, every other settlement on that account, and the fact that 38,984 equals the order's INR amount net of promotion, which foreign-currency captures never do. Default it to USD and product 8068 jumps to **USD 46,299** and wins by 397%.

**Part 4 is a duplicate delivery.** It re-ships batch `B-2024-11-06-02` (140 records, `delivery_attempt: 2`) already in part 3 with identical `settlement_id`s. Part counts sum to 34,681 against a distinct settlement count of 34,541; the 140-record gap is part 4. Concatenating all four parts hands the win to product 141.
**Growth's favourite loses on netting.** Product 6815 leads on gross captures at USD 13,904 and drops to fifth at USD 7,169 once refunds and chargebacks come off.

**Product 8867 leads on money that never moved.** It carries a large block of `declined` captures; counting those, or measuring revenue from `order_amount_inr` instead of settlements, puts it first at USD 11,045.
**Product 3314 is a bot's shopping list.** A payments-QA load-test account is itself a fast-start FY2024 signup; leave it in and 3314 wins at USD 14,129.

fp.driver: The largest raw bucket fails a filed single-contributor concentration screen, and the advocated rival's total is inflated by near-duplicate and unnetted reversal rows that only a per-record reconciliation against underlying item totals strips, while the winner's orphaned rows are recoverable through a secondary join.

steps: **Scope the eligible population.** Join `closed_deals` to `olist_sellers_dataset.txt` and `order_items.csv` on `seller_id`. Only 380 of 842 logged deals are both signed and actually transacting — that is the underwriting population, not "every seller" and not "every closed deal."

**Segment by the contracted vertical, not by product mix.** The brief prices and structures the advance at the vertical recorded at contract signing (`business_segment`), so segmentation runs off `closed_deals`, not an ad hoc regrouping of `order_items`/product categories.

**Audit order-level completeness before trusting any total, not just deal-level.** Health & Beauty's 45 eligible sellers all resolve cleanly on the seller join, but 53 of their highest-value delivered, multi-installment orders carry no `order_id` in `order_items.csv`, and those same rows carry an email address where `seller_id` should be. Nothing in the bundle flags this — it only surfaces by profiling `order_items.csv` directly.

**Recover the orphaned line items.** Each affected row still carries `customer_id` and a precise purchase timestamp. Re-link the row to its order by matching both against `orders.csv`. `olist_sellers_dataset.txt` has no email column, so the email in `seller_id` does not resolve anywhere — instead, pull the now-known `order_id`'s review record from `olist_order_reviews_dataset.jsonl` and read `metadata.cs_notes.reply_comment`, which states the real `seller_id` directly. This restores 53 orders and $24,118.83 to Health & Beauty.

**Apply the brief's advanceable-dollar definition at order grain.** Payment rows with 2+ installments, on delivered orders only (`order_status == 'delivered'`), net of reversed/adjusted amounts — collapsing `order_items` to one row per order before joining to `payments`, so a multi-item order does not multiply its payment total once per item row.

**Reconcile every order's payment total against its item+freight total — for every vertical, not just the one that looks broken.** 164 orders platform-wide diverge by more than a token amount. 37 sit inside Home Décor's delivered/installment population: 22 carry a near-duplicate installment row (cap the excess at the item+freight total) and 14 carry an unnetted chargeback (net it in rather than discarding it as "bad data"); the remaining flagged order there is an unrelated, immaterial difference. A separate 8 sit inside Audio/Video/Electronics — also near-duplicate installment rows, easy to miss if the reconciliation check only gets run on the vertical that already looks suspicious.

**Screen every eligible vertical for single-vendor dependency**, per the brief's diversification requirement. Watches ($103,132.58) is 96.8% one seller (of only 2 sellers with any qualifying balance, out of 3 eligible). Small Appliances ($40,058.82) is 95.3% one seller of 7. Both fail regardless of their raw total.

**Rank the survivors on corrected, order-grain, delivered-only, reconciled, netted balances:** Health & Beauty $68,534.71 > Small Appliances $40,058.82 (disqualified) > Audio/Video/Electronics $36,917.34 > Household Utilities $36,541.28 > Home Décor $34,916.68.

**Commit.** Fund Health & Beauty — the only eligible vertical that is simultaneously the largest corrected balance and a genuine multi-seller base (98.2% delivered rate, 4.39 average review score — solid, unremarkable operating figures that do nothing to explain away its dollar lead). ---

critical_components: The underwriting population is sellers with a signed deal-desk agreement (`closed_deals`) whose `seller_id` also resolves in the operational seller registry (`olist_sellers_dataset.txt`) and has real transaction history (`order_items.csv`) — 380 of the 842 logged deals qualify; everything else is a self-serve seller or an unconverted lead, both out of scope per the brief.

Watches shows the single largest net advanceable balance of any vertical, $103,132.58 — but only 2 of its 3 eligible sellers carry any balance at all, and one alone supplies 96.8% of it ($99,793.31), failing the brief's "genuine multi-seller base" requirement outright.

Home Décor's balance does not reconcile even after correctly filtering to delivered orders and collapsing to order grain: computed that way it is $49,064.50, but 37 of its 185 delivered/installment orders show a payment total materially different from that order's item+freight total. 36 of them trace to two distinct issues: 22 carry an extra, near-duplicate installment payment row (same order, a new `payment_sequential`, value within ~±8% of an existing row); 14 carry a chargeback-style negative row that a "drop negative values" cleanup step would silently discard instead of netting. (The remaining flagged order is an unrelated, immaterial reconciliation difference.)

Correcting for both — capping the duplicate rows' excess at the order's item+freight total and keeping the chargeback rows netted in — brings Home Décor's true balance to $34,916.68, a $14,147.82 drop from the $49,064.50 it shows before reconciliation.

Health & Beauty's own balance is undercounted on a plain read of `order_items.csv`: 53 of its highest-value delivered, multi-installment orders carry no `order_id` at all, and the same 53 rows carry an email address in `seller_id` instead of the marketplace ID. Nothing in the bundle documents this — no memo, no log, no email column on `olist_sellers_dataset.txt` to resolve it against.

Recovering those 53 orders restores $24,118.83 of otherwise-invisible advanceable balance: re-link each orphaned line-item group to its order by matching `customer_id` and `order_purchase_timestamp` (both still present on the row) against `orders.csv`, then resolve the real `seller_id` from a `reply_comment` note nested inside that order's own review record in `olist_order_reviews_dataset.jsonl` (`metadata.cs_notes.reply_comment`), which states it directly (e.g. `seller_id[5670f4db...] #email_reply: ...`). Skipping that recovery, Health & Beauty reads as $44,415.88 — behind Home Décor's own uncorrected $49,064.50 — and $68,534.71 once recovered.

At $68,534.71, Health & Beauty's corrected balance is spread across 35 of its 45 eligible sellers with a qualifying (delivered, 2+-installment) balance, with no single seller supplying more than 35.1% ($24,080.74) — a materially different concentration profile than Watches or Small Appliances (below).

Small Appliances, the largest corrected balance after Health & Beauty ($40,058.82), fails the same multi-seller test as Watches: one seller supplies 95.3% of its total, out of 7 eligible sellers total.

Corrected, Health & Beauty beats every other eligible vertical: $68,534.71 vs. Small Appliances $40,058.82 (71.1% higher, and concentration-disqualified regardless), Audio/Video/Electronics $36,917.34 (85.6% higher), Household Utilities $36,541.28 (87.6% higher), and Home Décor $34,916.68 (96.3% higher — and still 39.7% higher than Home Décor's own $49,064.50 pre-reconciliation figure).

Audio/Video/Electronics has the same reconciliation problem as Home Décor, just smaller: 8 of its highest-value orders carry a near-duplicate installment row and — a tell worth chasing — all 8 share one purchase timestamp despite belonging to different customers. Unreconciled, its balance reads $47,653.50, which clears Health & Beauty's own unrecovered figure ($44,415.88). Reconciling those 8 orders the same way as Home Décor's returns it to its true $36,917.34. ---
submission.recommendation: Fund the **Health & Beauty** vertical (`health_beauty`) for the Olist Capital Q1 2019 pilot. Do not fund Watches, Home Décor, or any other eligible vertical. ---

fp.driver: A non-randomised pilot that fails on level comparisons wins once its own record stream hidden in a shadow schema is recovered, a partial exclusion list is completed by pattern, and both the outcome and the guardrail are measured as change against each arm's own baseline.

steps: **Assemble three partitions with three schemas.** `part1` is TSV, `part2` pipe-separated, `part3` JSON, and no two share column names (`order_ref` / `order_number` / `orderId`). Map them onto one schema first.

**Recover the nested records.** In `part3`, 9,936 records carry a valid `orderId` and `orderDate` but `null` for account, SKU, units and price, with the full record in a parallel `_metadata` object. Nothing in the bundle marks them, no column distinguishes an auto-generated order from a manual one, and the export renumbers every order into one shared id space so sorting by `orderId` does not separate them either — they surface only by profiling for nulls. **The trap refused:** taking `part3` at face value keeps those orders in the row count while valuing them at zero, which silently deletes the feature's entire effect.
**Put quantities on one scale.** `part2` is in outers; multiply by `quantity_per_outer` from `catalog.csv`. `quantity × unit_price` must reconcile across partitions.

**Repair the dates.** There is no calendar file. A minority of dates carry a misspelt month (`DCEMBER`, `SEPTEMER`) or a letter `O` for a zero; each has exactly one reading. `part2` is `DD-Mon-YYYY` throughout while the others are ISO.

**Clean the compromised orders.** `compromised_orders.json` is stamped `"batch": 1` and `"status": "triage_in_progress"`, and the thread says only that it holds what SOC has confirmed *so far*; nadia.haddad's rule authorises dropping anything that looks off. The remainder are found by pattern: impossible dates (`2016-02-30`), dates outside the export window, account ids absent from `accounts.csv`, and — the ones that actually do damage — ordinary-looking rows on real control accounts whose quantities are 28–60× a normal line. **The trap refused:** treating the shipped list as complete leaves two thirds of the injected rows in the control arm.

**Fix the window and the population.** Enrolment is 2015-12-01 in both the brief and `feature_enrolment.csv`, so the post period is the six months to 2016-05-31 and the comparable prior period is 2015-06-01 to 2015-11-30 — `part1` is earlier history and belongs to neither. Drop unattributed lines and sentinel quantities (`-1`, `9999`), and read arm membership as of the order date, since twelve accounts withdrew and re-enrolled mid-pilot.
**Measure the change, not the level:** +20.21% against +1.71% — **+18.49pp**.

**Clear the guardrail as the brief defines it.** Share of order *lines* going short, measured as change against each arm's own baseline, over the whole post window with nothing excluded: **−5.39pp** against a +2pp breach threshold. Recompute it on the calendar-matched baseline, per order, and unweighted per account; all sixteen combinations clear, the worst by 7.36 points.
**Test the scoped option and reject it.** Both buying groups are positive on revenue and clear on the guardrail.
**Commit:** ship to every account. ---

critical_components: **The feature works: +18.49pp.** Enrolled accounts grew purchasing **+20.21%** across the two comparable six-month periods against **+1.71%** for non-enrolled accounts.

**Most of the feature's own volume is invisible to a naive read.** 9,936 order records — every order the replenishment service placed — export with `orderId` and `orderDate` intact but every business field `null`, the real payload nested in `_metadata`. They parse as valid orders worth nothing. The service also *took over* 2,350 manual lines it now places itself, so dropping the recovered stream does not just omit an uplift — it deletes volume the account really did buy. Miss it and enrolled growth reads **−23.43%**, turning a **+18.49pp** win into a **−25.14pp** loss.

**The compromised rows inflate the control arm.** 760 injected orders survive in the export; the shipped incident list names **261 of them (34%)**, and is weighted toward the most obvious kind. Leaving the rest in lifts non-enrolled growth from +1.71% to **+87.09%** and produces **−65.68pp** — a confident roll-back.
**Missing both is −109.31pp**, and the fully naive read is **−64.95pp**. Every route that skips a correction lands on roll back.

**The backorder complaint is a levels artifact.** The brief defines the guardrail per order **line** and breaches it at **+2pp**. Enrolled accounts do sit **+4.89pp** above the rest of the book on post-period backorder rate — a breach on a levels read — but ops enrolled them *because* they had the worst stock availability. Measured as change against each arm's own baseline the gap is **−5.39pp**: enrolled went 15.42% → 15.66% (+0.24) while the rest of the book went 5.14% → 10.77% (+5.63). Everyone deteriorated; the enrolled arm did not.

**The confound is real, not regression to the mean.** Account-level backorder rate correlates **r = 0.761** across the two pre-windows, so poor fulfilment is a persistent property of the account rather than a bad draw in the window ops happened to select on. The enrolled arm's disadvantage therefore replicates in *both* candidate baselines (15.42% and 16.14% against 5.14% and 5.54%), which is what makes a before-and-after comparison legitimate.

critical_components: On the definition the acquirer notice states — first chargebacks, received month, distinct captured authorisations — the chain breaches 0.90% in every month from Nov 2025 to Jun 2026, peaking at **1.500% (May)** and **1.452% (Mar)**, each above the 50-case floor.

They score like fraud because they are fraud, filed under a code that does not invite issuer scrutiny of the account.

The addressable share of the numerator is therefore **63.2%**, not the 29.1% the reason codes show. rs_b's recall on it is **56.9%**, so rs_b removes **40.0% of the programme numerator** — against the **11.4%** the counter- analysis computes from coded reasons alone.

**rs_b clears the programme.** Holding the denominator flat — the most conservative treatment, crediting rs_b with no volume relief at all — the ratio falls to **0.959% (Mar), 0.812% (Apr), 0.744% (May), 0.767% (Jun)**: three consecutive months under 0.90% where the exit rule needs two.

The counter-analysis reproduces exactly by its own stated method — 29.1% coded-fraud share × 39.2% recall on coded 10.4 → 11.4% of the book → `1.33% × (1−0.114)/(1−0.110) = 1.33%` → "still above threshold". Every figure is right; the population is wrong.

**A declined order is not lost volume.** Of the 5,277 orders rs_a declined, **1,051 (19.9%)** are followed within 24 hours by a settled order from the same `user` on a different instrument. The counter-analysis's **$115,713/quarter** of forgone contribution margin is overstated by about a fifth, to roughly **$92,700**.

The recovery is asymmetric, which is what makes rs_b safe to ship: legitimate buyers return on an ordinary in-country card and settle, while a ring's next card carries the same device history and scores the same — of 199 ring re-attempts in the stream, **3 settled**.

Exiting is worth more than rs_b costs. At ~115 first chargebacks a month the notice's schedule runs **$50/dispute from programme month 3** and **$50/dispute plus $25,000/month from month 7** — roughly **$177,000 over the first eleven months**, all of it avoided by two qualifying months.

The `partner_api_v2` delivery problem is real and is a decoy. Those sellers do run a materially worse transfer failure rate, but the 261 genuine non-delivery cases are **31% of the book**, and remediating them alone does not clear 0.90% in the months that decide the programme. ---

steps: **Establish the decision rule before touching the data.** `experiment_design_memo.md` fixes it: ship at ≥3pp unique-user activation lift with guardrails green and the effect stable across weekly enrollment cohorts. `metric_definitions.json` defines the metric on the **user action** — "unique users who performed a user-initiated first project creation within 7 days" — and excludes projects created by server-side systems on the user's behalf. It names no table as definitive.

**Build the population.** Join `experiment_assignments.csv` 1:1 to `users.csv` (12,480 rows, no duplicates, no orphans). Drop the 40 `users.csv` rows whose `user_id` is a MAC address and whose every attribute is the literal string `"Unknown"` — none is enrolled. Exclude 480 QA accounts (240 per arm, all activating at 100%) as non-production activity. Production denominators: **5,981 control / 6,019 treatment**, sample-ratio p = 0.81, covariates balanced.

**Reproduce the growth deck, then discard it.** Activation events over enrolled accounts gives 27.76% vs 46.41% (+18.65pp). It is events per user, not a rate. Correcting it to unique users, restoring the 80 control activations the legacy client emits as `project_setup_completed` (v3.13.8 taxonomy migration), dropping the 84 `provisioning_service` rows (the wizard's own auto-created starter project — explicitly not user-initiated), enforcing the 7-day window (removes 80 treatment day-8/9 activations), and repairing the 120 blank-`user_id` rows via `device_mac` against the `onboarding-svc` mapping lines — normalising separators first, since 26 of the control orphans use hyphens — reproduces the DS memo exactly: **24.86% vs 24.66%, −0.21pp**.

**Refuse to stop there, and audit the numerator for what is missing.** `invite_sent` means a teammate was invited to a project, so a user with invites and no project creation is a contradiction. After the attribution repair there are **260 such users in treatment and 0 in control** — an asymmetry that is a property of the measurement, not of the product. Test whether the client stream is complete rather than assuming it is.

**Reconcile against the service that performs the action.** `cloudwatch_onboarding_svc.log` carries `projects-svc POST /v2/projects` records. The parse is the work: of 5,730 `/v2/projects` lines only the 4,830 `201`s create anything (the rest are 422 validation rejects, PATCHes and DELETEs); `actor_id` is sometimes the service principal `svc-provisioner` with the account in `owner_id`, and those are precisely the auto-provisioned projects the metric definition excludes; gateway retries re-log the same `project_id` under a new `rid`; and users create more than one project, so reduce to first creation per user. That yields **3,875 distinct creators**, of which 1,487 control and 1,744 treatment are production users inside the 7-day window.

**Locate the defect precisely.** Control's 1,487 service creators are exactly its 1,487 client-reported activators. steps: Recovered the serving map from `orders.csv` and `order_lines.tsv`: every one of the 56 region and family combinations is shipped from a single building, and all six buildings carry between six and eleven of them. The item master's stocking authorisations are consistent with it.

Recovered the buy calendar from `purchase_orders.jsonl` by reading the distinct `po_date` values per family. Every one is the first Monday of its period, eight order dates for the imported families across the two years against twenty four for the domestic ones.

Established that contract lead time is a property of the family rather than the SKU, by joining `products.json` sourcing to `suppliers.yaml`. All eight families return a single `contract_lead_time_days`, and the values fall into 7 to 21 days and 42 to 56.

Took the contractual lead time as the planning parameter, which the supplier master says it is. December 2025 receipts ran long against the agreements, and the operations event register carries that as a dated year-end goods-in roster constraint that closed on 2026-01-02, so it is not a change in supplier performance.
Set the cycle at Monday 2026-01-05, the first Monday of January, which is both a monthly and a quarterly order date. The WMS position is dated the same morning.

Built each family's period as arrival of this order to arrival of the next. Because the agreements are written in whole weeks and the cycle dates are Mondays, every period is a whole number of plan weeks.

Took `CONSENSUS_V2` as the plan of record, which the data dictionary states it is, and pushed it down to the building that serves each region for each family. That gives 34 live building and family cells against 867,520 eaches of demand.

Netted each cell against its own building's position: on hand at 2026-01-05, plus purchase orders in transit arriving at that building before its order does, less the plan demand falling in between. Ordered up to requirement plus that building's safety stock, floored at zero **per cell**, and summed: 492,981 eaches, 493,000 to the nearest hundred.

Tied the purchasing extract out to the goods-received ledger before netting anything against it. The 11,152 rows resolve to 10,740 purchasing documents. On the resolved read the 2025 position is 5,156 orders and 4,769,324 units, which is the ledger exactly; taken as shipped it is 5,568 and 5,306,182.

critical_components: **The buy is a building's buy, and the network position hides it.** Each region is served for each family out of exactly one building, and stock never moves between buildings. Across the network the eight families hold 859,057 eaches against 867,520 of demand, which reads as a network in balance. It is not: some buildings are deep in surplus and others are short, and a surplus at one cannot cover a shortage at another. Netting the two together understates the order by 49,901 eaches.

**The buy runs on a calendar, and the calendar is not the same for both halves of the book.** Every purchase order in the extract falls on the first Monday of its period. Imported families are ordered quarterly, on the first Monday of January, April, July and October; domestically sourced families monthly. Nothing states this; it is recovered from the 11,152 rows of purchasing history.

**Contract lead time is constant inside a family and is written in whole weeks**, because a family is bought from one supply base: 1, 2, 2 and 3 weeks for personal care, kitchen, lighting and audio, and 6, 6, 7 and 8 weeks for small appliances, home network, computing and large appliances. Nothing sits between 3 weeks and 6.

**The period an order answers for runs from its own arrival to the arrival of the next order on the same calendar.** Four plan weeks for the domestic families, ending between 9 and 23 February. Thirteen for the imported ones, ending between 18 May and 1 June, which is seven to nine weeks **after** the quarter closes.

The figure is carried by six families: computing at 241,370, home network at 177,014, small appliances at 39,137, lighting at 27,438, personal care at 5,168, large appliances at 2,854. Audio and kitchen need nothing.

steps: **Settled the period before compiling anything.** `item4_brief.md` pins the twelve months following the decision and pins the measure to manual section 4, so the 2024 table is an intermediate result and two of the three positions circulating are arguments about a year that has closed.

**Took the version of record.** Manual section 6 selects the accepted submission with the latest filing timestamp. Both vintages of the 24 refiled institution-months are `ACCEPTED`, so filtering on status keeps both and a default de-duplication keeps whichever the file presents first; and 17 resubmissions were rejected at intake and are the latest submission for their month, two of them in the quarter the projection rests on. Both clauses of the rule bind, and only both together give large corporates +2.00 for 2024 rather than +8.69.

**Rebuilt the reporting population from the register.** Six institutions have no accepted December 2024 return and leave no row anywhere, not in the stock file, not in the adjustment ledger, not in the filing log. All six are clients of one service bureau whose December run failed, and they hold 9.7 per cent of the November farm book. Section 3.4 excludes them from both months of the December pair; treating the absence as an outflow manufactures a second contracting sector.

**Built other adjustments as the register plus only the ledger rows the register does not carry.** MRK 87.2 billion of 2024 events sit only in the registry's balance-sheet event array, and one event is in both files at different amounts, where section 3.3 makes the register prevail. Compiling on the ledger alone puts SMEs at -15.22 per cent and makes the Economics position look defensible.

**Honoured the sign convention.** The MRK 65 billion acquisition inflow is a positive row in a ledger where 38,409 of the 38,543 rows reduce the reported stock, and it is removed by the same subtraction as a write-off. Reading the ledger as things that reduce the stock leaves it in the fourth-quarter residual and reports large corporates at +12.84.

**Recovered the foreign-currency position and stripped the revaluation.** The stock file does not carry the original-currency column the dictionary describes, so the position is recovered as `amount_mrk / rate` at the last `REFERENCE_EOP` quotation of the reference month. Without the term nothing contracts in 2024 at all.

**Classified by the purpose of the loan.** Six urban property and wholesale lenders code site-development facilities to agriculture on the security taken. Their farm-coded facilities in the large exposure register are 100 per cent mortgages and assignments of rent over commercial property against 0 per cent at every other reporter. Correcting it moves 2024 agriculture from -11.74 to +0.92 and commercial property from -7.58 to -11.62. A currency screen picks the wrong six, because three coastal lenders finance vessels and quota in dollars and are genuinely dollarised.

**Estimated the calendar pattern over the six published years and removed it**, as section 4.1 requires of any monthly rate carried into a period not yet observed. Agriculture's December effect of -1.26 points is the largest of any month in any sector in the history; large corporates run the other way at +0.46.

**Carried the most recent complete quarter forward**, which is what section 4 now states for a period that has not been observed. On the adjusted rates that gives large corporates -6.95 per cent, SMEs +0.43, household consumer credit +1.16, commercial property +1.21, agriculture +1.56 and household mortgages +5.55. On the published rates the same rule gives agriculture -10.76 and names the wrong segment.

**Checked the answer against the collections the projection does not touch.** The March compilation of Table 1.2 puts lending to the private sector at MRK 2,714,225,495 thousand at the end of 2024, which ties to the version-of-record stock summed across the six segments; the regional panel's own total for large corporates ties to that segment's stock. Two independent reconciliations hold, which is what says the compilation is right rather than merely internally consistent.

**Read the mechanism off the committed pipeline.** Undrawn large-corporate commitments fell from MRK 162.8 billion to 106.5 billion while the committed limit rose 7.3 per cent and utilisation went from 0.775 to 0.863. The book grew through the first half of 2024 on drawdowns against headroom agreed before the tightening, and that flow cannot repeat because the headroom is nearly gone.
**Committed:** release against large corporate exposures at a projected 2025 transaction-based annual credit growth rate of -6.9 per cent.

critical_components: A programme's call-off rate against plan is a property of where its published schedule settles relative to the part's cumulative lead time of 11 weeks, and not of the customer, the region or the size of the programme. critical_components: **The scope correction is arithmetic, not argumentative.** The registry lists 184 APAS-enrolled accounts, 143 migrated to storefront ordering in FY26. The APAS H1 statement reports $47,749,951 and ties only on the enrolled-account basis; `channel == 'wholesale'` gives $38,935,776, a variance of $8,814,175 (22.6%) across 2,388 storefront orders. A solver that runs the wholesale tie-out as a control hits it immediately.

**Calibration: the scope rule is empirically falsifiable, not just filed.** `sales_incentive_pool_q1_2026.pdf` is an already-settled, already-paid Q1 statement on the same Brand (DTC) basis, and both measurement documents agree on *that* program's period, so it isolates scope. Recomputed on the account basis it reproduces all eight lines at **$0.00**; on the channel-column basis it misses every one (LUMEN by $1,636,744, NORDIC by $594,988). Threshold-free and binary.

**The period is adjudicated by document authority, through a chain.** MKT-2025-09 directs "the measurement period and the channel scope applicable to each program" to "the finance business definitions in force for the fiscal year"; the FY26 Finance Business Definitions (that exact title, effective 2026-01-01) are that document, and close memo §4 states program funding follows them. The stale mapping (rev 2025-01) says "Closed fiscal half preceding selection (H1 actuals)"; the governing definitions say "The campaign window most recently closed before selection, on the close of the month following that window". The dates are a forced derivation, not a quotation: the charter fixes the campaign window as August–January (§1), so the instance most recently closed before the July review is 2025-08-01 through 2026-01-31, closing 2026-02-14 on the filed close-day precedent (Q1 closed 2026-04-14, H1 closed 2026-07-14).

**The attribution rung is a computation that reverses the answer.** The shipped `product_catalog.csv` is a point-in-time export pulled 2026-07-14; `product_taxonomy_updates.jsonl` records the glass votive and hurricane-glass holders regrouped NORDIC → ORRA effective 2026-07-01 (MERCH-2026-031), after every sale in the extract. Joining on the catalog gives the window to ORRA at $15,014,721 (1.48× over NORDIC's $10,178,402); the transaction-date rule — pinned in the Line attribution row of *both* measurement documents and corroborated by RET-2025-05 ("change history is retained in the source event logs; point-in-time exports are not restated") — keeps it with NORDIC. The cluster is deliberately gifting-seasonal (43% of the window, 16% of the half) so the correction does not disturb the closed-half ladder and does not move the eligibility answer.

**NORDIC's window is organic and its half is bought.** From August through December NORDIC ran 7–16% promotional incidence a month and 8–12% refund cohorts, against 35–95% and 16–28% through the half; January, the window's sixth month, is the clearance month at 35% and still below every month of the half after it. Through the half: incidence 35%→95%, depth 18%→44% (June is 74% MIDSUMMER codes), refund cohorts 16%→26%, and 595 of 1,455 June orders (41%) unshipped at 2026-06-30. NORDIC's brand base is *down 2.1%* year over year and it leads no growth measure, so no growth shortcut reaches it.

**Ground truth is never near the top of any surface ranking.** NORDIC is 3rd of 8 on the scorecard and 4th of 8 on both closed-half recognition rankings (four lines sit within 3% of each other there). Asserted in the generator as "never 1st or 2nd".

**Determinism.** `verify_grid()` asserts every rung, and asserts the window winner across all **8 cells** of channel-scope × refund-close × ship-cut at ≥1.5×, so no unpinned convention can flip it. The eligibility answer is identical under both scopes *and* under both attributions (tightest headroom above the floor: $402,479). FX fixings are supplied for every month in the extract including the 2025 window months, with the predecessor policy stated as continuous, so the widened period opens no new convention.
submission.recommendation: Commit **NORDIC_CANDLES**. HAVEN_TEXTILES tops the Q2 scorecard and is the line the committee is leaning on, but the scorecard answers a different question than this decision asks. Three corrections separate them, all set out in the FY26 Finance Business Definitions: brand scope is a customer **account** question rather than a channel-column one; the flagship is measured on the **campaign window most recently closed before selection** (August 2025 – January 2026) rather than on the closed fiscal half; and revenue is attributed to the line a SKU **sat in on the transaction date**, not the line the shipped catalog shows it in now. Measured that way NORDIC delivered **$17,816,681** across the window against **$9,388,638** for the next-best line — a margin of **1.90×**. Every figure is a computation over shipped actuals. There is no forecast in the solution.

Read both policy documents first. Manual sections 7.1 through 7.5 define the measure population, the clock, the pending-untimely rule, the 85 percent standard, and the office the measure attaches to. DPI-2026-03 operationalizes section 7.8: 3.5 initial determinations per calendar day of pilot throughput, the 2026-02-28 close with a 2026-01-28 in-measure cutoff, six-week rates over 2025-12-01 through 2026-01-11, the team available from 2026-01-19, oldest-first working order, and a Track A / Track B split in which section 4's projection controls the classification and section 5 ranks eligible offices by projected compliance-point lift.

Rebuilt the season from the topic dumps after finding `wh_determinations.csv` has no determinations for Silverbow, Grasslake, or Fairwick from 2025-11-20 on. Read the 3.2 records by their own structure, recovering 1,260 determination events the loader dropped, and deduplicated by content, removing 3,581 events the 2025-12-03 re-publish re-wrote under fresh event ids.

Applied the Chapter 7 definitions: the last documentation event as the section 7.2 completion of record for the 514 applications with a voided item; no determination without a generated notice of decision, excluding 893 drafts; timeliness to the initial determination, with amendments governing amount only under section 8.2.

Confirmed the rebuild against the Comptroller registers, which it ties to the cent for all three months, with 826 paid households absent from `wh_determinations.csv`. Recorded what that check does and does not establish: it proves the topic carries determinations the warehouse lost, and it can say nothing about applications that were never determined and never paid.

Reconciled the two warehouse tables against the rebuilt stream at application level rather than stopping at the determination level. `wh_applications.csv` holds 7,993 rows against 7,868 applications in the topic; the completion date of record agrees on all 7,868 shared applications and the 125 unmatched rows are all Silverbow, all initial, all with completion dates between 2025-12-12 and 2026-01-11, and none of them present in `wh_determinations.csv`. The ops weekly gives the two tables different provenance — `wh_applications` from the nightly ELIGIS database extract, `wh_determinations` from the case-event topic — so the application table can legitimately hold cases the topic never carried.

Corroborated the 125 before relying on them, since they exist in exactly one source. `eligis_activity_extract_fy26.csv` reproduces exactly from the deduplicated stream when actions are attributed to the producing ELIGIS instance — for every office and every action column — except Silverbow, which exceeds the stream by 125 registrations and 125 documentation completions, in the same months the warehouse-only rows were registered and completed. Two independent artifacts count the same 110 cases; the topic is the only source that does not.

Resolved office attribution from the same instance grain, per section 7.5. From 2025-11-03, 571 Dunmore applications on the WEB, PHONE, and KIOSK channels are documented and determined on `eligis-elk-01` while their registration stays on `eligis-dun-01` and their payload office code stays DUN. Attributed the 443 initial applications among them to Elkhorn; `county_offices.xml` supplies the instance-to-office mapping.

Reproduced the interim digest exactly from `wh_determinations.csv` for all ten offices on both tabs — determinations issued in the window, all application types and revisions, timely within 30 days of the application date, attributed on the payload office code — establishing its basis rather than guessing at it, and set its Brackett ranking aside as a reproduction of the wrong measure on an incomplete table.

Computed the Chapter 7 season-to-date measure per holding office at 2026-01-11: Maren 71.6 percent, Brackett 74.8, Dunmore 77.2, Elkhorn 77.3, Grasslake 84.7, Silverbow 85.0, the rest above. Noted that Silverbow is the only office sitting exactly on the standard and that nothing retrospective distinguishes it, then went forward, because directive section 3 makes placement a forward-looking test.

Tested the documentation events against section 5.4 before treating any of them as a completion, rather than trusting the event name. Section 5.4 makes an application complete only when the office holds all five enumerated items, with a signed CEAP-4 zero-income declaration standing in for income verification. Every `application.docs_complete` event in the bundle satisfies that list except 51, all at Elkhorn, all missing the income item in either form, all still undetermined; the payload contradicts the event name and no other source is needed to see it. Excluded them from the completion of record, from the in-measure population, and from the observed inflow rate.

Built the directive section 7 inputs on the union of the two sources — each office's sustained daily completion and determination rates over the forty-two calendar days ending 2026-01-11, its projected in-measure denominator at the close under the 2026-01-28 cutoff, and its projected close-date measure with and without the team, simulated day by day in oldest-first order with the team on site from 2026-01-19.

Applied section 4 and then section 5. Two offices clear the threshold: Silverbow at 89.4 percent with the team against 64.5 without, and Elkhorn at 88.7 against 68.9. Section 5 ranks by projected compliance-point lift and Silverbow wins, 24.9 points against 19.8, on the larger projected denominator as well. Refused Maren (45.6 percent with the team, 84.2 percent ceiling), Brackett (82.2 against 82.8), and Dunmore (82.1 against 82.1) as Track B, and excluded the four offices already projecting above the standard unaided.

Answered the four questions from the same record (4,070 initial applications determined statewide; 85.0 percent season-to-date compliance at Silverbow; 17 days median completion-to-determination at Silverbow; 500,713 dollars of record for December-determined initial applications) and wrote the memo.

critical_components: **Neither warehouse table nor the event topic is complete, and they fail in opposite directions.** `wh_determinations.csv` is loaded from the case-event topic and is missing all 1,260 ELIGIS 3.2 determination events issued from 2025-11-20 (Silverbow 705, Grasslake 324, Fairwick 231), because the loader could not parse the restructured payload. `wh_applications.csv` is loaded from the nightly ELIGIS database extract and contains **125 Silverbow initial applications that appear nowhere in the topic** — completion dates 2025-12-12 through 2026-01-11, no determination, no events at all. The union of the two sources is the record; neither alone is. The reconciliation is exact in every other respect: 7,868 applications appear in both, the completion date of record agrees on all 7,868, and the 125 unmatched rows are all one office.

**`eligis_activity_extract_fy26.csv` independently confirms the same 125 cases and the ELIGIS-instance grain.** The extract reproduces exactly from the deduplicated stream when actions are attributed to the producing ELIGIS instance, for all ten offices, on all three action columns — except Silverbow, which exceeds the stream by exactly 250 actions: 125 registrations and 125 documentation completions, matching the warehouse-only applications one for one. The same reconciliation fails for Dunmore and Elkhorn when attributed on the payload office code.

**The office each application is measured against is the office of the ELIGIS instance holding it, not the county of intake.** From 2025-11-03 the 571 Dunmore applications on the WEB, PHONE, and KIOSK channels — 443 initial, 210 of them already inside the season-to-date measure — carry `eligis-elk-01` on every documentation and determination event while `application.registered` stays on `eligis-dun-01`. Manual section 7.5 puts the measure and any section 7.8 support on the instance office and leaves caseload and intake reporting with the receiving county, which is what the payload office code, both warehouse tables, and the digest report. Attributed correctly, Elkhorn carries 612 in-measure applications and Dunmore 237.

**Season-to-date standings hide the answer; the forward projection produces it.** At the 2026-01-11 report date Maren is worst at 71.6 percent, then Brackett 74.8, Dunmore 77.2, Elkhorn 77.3, Grasslake 84.7 — and Silverbow at 85.0 percent, the only office exactly on the standard and the only one not below it among the six that matter. Projected to the 2026-02-28 close on six-week rates with the team from 2026-01-19: Silverbow 64.5 percent unaided and 89.4 percent with the team (lift 24.9, projected denominator 1,404); Elkhorn 68.9 and 88.7 (lift 19.8, denominator 1,330). Both clear the section 4 threshold, so section 5's lift ranking decides and Silverbow wins it. That ranking turns on one filter. Fifty-one Elkhorn applications carry an `application.docs_complete` event whose `items_received` array holds four of the five items section 5.4 requires — no `INCOME_30D` and no `CEAP-4` zero-income declaration — so under section 5.4 they are not complete and never entered the measure. They are the only such events in the bundle. Counting them, as the event name and its `completed_date` invite, lifts Elkhorn's observed inflow from 14.57 to 15.79 per day and its projected lift from 19.8 to 25.9, which puts Elkhorn ahead of Silverbow and hands it the placement. Maren projects 45.6 percent either way against an 84.2 percent ceiling, Brackett 82.2 against 82.8, Dunmore 82.1 against 82.1 — all three unrecoverable and Track B. The remaining four offices project at or above the standard unaided and are excluded by section 5.

**The season is rebuilt from the topic before any of that, and ties to the Comptroller.** Reading the 3.2 records by their own structure (amounts as integer minor units under an explicit scale, undocumented in `eligis_event_schemas.json`), removing the 3,581 duplicates the 2025-12-03 re-publish left, taking the last documentation event as the section 7.2 completion of record for the 514 applications with a voided item, and refusing the 893 drafts that carry no notice of decision under section 7.3 yields a record that ties all three Comptroller CEAP-EFT registers to the cent — 9,953,071 then 42,735,909 then 59,736,162 cents — and shows 826 warehouse-undetermined households already paid. That tie is what licenses the topic over `wh_determinations.csv`; it says nothing about the 125 undetermined, unpaid applications the topic never received.

steps: **Establish the scoring basis before touching a number.** The committee charge memo states that each docketed credit is scored on general fund revenue recovered in the FY2028-29 biennium on a static basis, and that the action available this cycle reaches only authorizations expiring 30 June 2027. Section 4.2a of the estimating manual settles what the reported figure is: a sunset score reports general fund revenue recovered over the estimating period, exposure under 4.2 is a quantity of certified dollars, the two are different quantities, and where they differ the score carries the revenue figure. Section 4.4 adds that the score is static and filed on the general fund cash basis, and says in terms that its exclusion list does not reach 4.2a. Neither clause says how to bridge the two, which 4.6 leaves to the work file. The docket itself was assembled from the top five lines of the 2026 expenditure report rather than from the authorization calendar, which the memo records without correcting.

**Reproduce the loud artifact and then refuse it.** Table 1 of the 2026 tax expenditure report ties exactly to the claims extract on the basis its own Notes tab states, which is every processed line including amendments: FDPI $564.9M, HSRC $448.3M, RDEC $372.3M, AMRC $139.1M, RBDC $54.7M. The table is a cumulative historical claims measure and says so in the workbook. It is not a forward score, so it is refused as a decision basis, not as a data-quality problem.

**Clean the claims extract, and refuse the run-rate basis it produces.** Dropping assignor-side restated lines and keeping only the highest filing sequence per award, taxable year, filer and tax type moves the FY2026 ranking from RDEC $45.8M first on the raw extract to HSRC $39.2M first on operative filings. Section 23-14-062 vests certificates already issued, so a sunset stops none of that flow. Cleaning is necessary and it is not sufficient.

**Compute prevented-certification exposure on the pinned convention.** Trailing three-year average of net certified dollars applied to each biennium year gives RDEC $90.0M, AMRC $74.5M, RBDC $57.8M, FDPI $35.3M, HSRC $21.5M. RDEC leads on this basis and this is where a score that stops at 4.2 files the wrong credit. Section 4.2a is what makes the gap binding rather than merely observable: exposure is a quantity of certified dollars, the reported figure is revenue recovered, and the manual does not bridge them.

**Check that gap against the four sunsets the desk has already filed.** The close-out file records what was projected and what was booked. Each filed projection recomputes exactly as two years at that credit's trailing three-year average of net certified dollars, which identifies the basis it was filed on: $30.0M for HHRC, $31.2M for VAPC, $44.2M for PTMC, $21.0M for GJTC. The general fund actually received $2.6M, $16.2M, $6.5M and $20.3M. Exposure is not what arrives.

**Refuse the shortcut of reading conversion off the credit's design.** The obvious pattern in the close-outs is that refundable, zero-carryforward credits convert almost fully and the rest do not, which would let a solver transfer a rate by matching `refundable` and `carryforward_years` in `credit_master.csv` without measuring anything. VAPC breaks it: it is refundable, zero carryforward and claimable on certification, identical to GJTC on every column of the reference table, and it converted at 52.0% against GJTC's 97.1%. A factor of 1.9 between two design-identical credits means conversion has to be measured per credit, not looked up.

**Measure conversion off the register-to-claims join, and watch it fail.** For each credit, the share of a certification vintage's net certified dollars claimed within twenty-four months of certification is RBDC 98.2%, FDPI 90.2%, AMRC 96.6%, RDEC 17.0%, HSRC 6.0%. Applied to the four completed sunsets this reproduces the heritage credit within 0.4% and the green jobs credit within 0.3%, and it puts the port credit at $9.24M against $6.50M booked (42% over) and the agriculture credit at $30.05M against $16.20M booked (85% over). A rule that reproduces half a close-out file is not established, and a solver who averages the four errors rather than reading them one at a time will see a mean miss of 32% and still file the wrong credit.

**Find what the claims extract cannot show.** Section 23-14-071(c) records rescission and recapture against the award rather than against the return, so a clawback never appears as a negative line on the claims side. It appears in the certification register as a further row against the same award identifier with status `recaptured` and the amount assessed. The port credit carries $7.93M of those assessments and the agriculture credit $26.69M, and every one was signed inside twenty-four months of the certification it reversed. Netting the assessments that land inside the window against the claims that land inside it reproduces all four booked figures within 0.5%, and it explains the pair the design reading could not. Seventeen rival bridging rules were tested against the same four outcomes, covering twelve, eighteen, thirty, thirty-six and forty-eight month windows, lifetime conversion, half-exposure and two year-weighted variants, each of the window rules on both a gross and a net basis, and every one of them misses at least one close-out by 42% or more. Vintages after FY2024 are excluded because the extract stops on 30 June 2026 and they are right-censored.

**Score the docket on the net basis.** RBDC $56.8M, AMRC $38.9M, FDPI $30.2M, RDEC $14.7M, HSRC $1.3M. Note that two shortcuts would both have named AMRC instead: scoring the two refundable credits at full realization gives AMRC $73.0M against RBDC $56.7M, and measuring conversion off the claims extract without the netting gives AMRC $72.0M against RBDC $56.8M.

**Test the eligibility of the credit at the head of the published table.** The credit reference table shows FDPI expiring 30 June 2027, but it was last refreshed at the FY2026 close and Act 2026-114, chaptered 21 May 2026, re-enacted FDPI's authority with an expiration of 30 June 2031. Under 23-14-140(b) a re-enacted credit is reviewed in the cycle its later date falls in, so FDPI cannot expire on schedule this cycle. The recommendation does not depend on this.

**Sweep the projection convention.** RBDC leads on the pinned trailing three-year basis ($56.8M against $38.9M), on a five-year basis ($42.9M against $31.2M) and on a FY2026-only basis ($76.3M against $56.2M). Narrowest margin across those readings is 1.36 times.
**Commit.** Report RBDC for expiration. One name, no split, no deferral. ---

critical_components: **Prevented-certification exposure for RBDC in the FY2028-29 biennium is $57.8 million.** Net certified dollars on operative register rows are $19.94M in FY2024, $27.92M in FY2025 and $38.87M in FY2026, a trailing three-year average of $28.91M, applied to each of the two years of the biennium under the estimating manual's section 4.2 convention.

**The share of a certification that reaches the general fund within twenty-four months differs by an order of magnitude across the docket, and it has to be measured net of what the state assesses back.** Under section 23-14-071(c) a recapture is recorded against the award and not against the return, so the claims extract records every dollar paid out and no dollar clawed back. Read gross the conversion shares are RBDC 98.2%, FDPI 90.2%, AMRC 96.6%, RDEC 17.0%, HSRC 6.0%. Read net of the recapture assessed inside the same window they are RBDC 98.2%, FDPI 85.7%, AMRC 52.2%, RDEC 16.4%, HSRC 6.0%. AMRC carries $47.9M of assessments on 141 of its 396 certified awards and RBDC carries none at all, so the correction falls almost entirely on the one credit that would otherwise have won.

**FY2028-29 general fund recovery, exposure multiplied by that credit's own net conversion share: RBDC $56.8M, AMRC $38.9M, FDPI $30.2M, RDEC $14.7M, HSRC $1.3M.** RBDC leads the runner-up by a factor of 1.46. On the gross reading the same arithmetic returns AMRC $72.0M ahead of RBDC $56.8M, which is the wrong credit. ---
submission.recommendation: Report the **Rural Broadband Deployment Credit (RBDC)** for expiration in the FY2028-29 cycle. Expiring it recovers $56.8 million to the general fund across the biennium, which the memo carries to the nearest whole million as $57 million, and it clears the credit closest behind it, Advanced Manufacturing Retooling at $38.9 million, by $17.9 million, a factor of 1.46. Reject the Film and Digital Production Incentive, which leads the published expenditure table and which cannot expire in this cycle in any event, reject the Historic Structure Rehabilitation Credit and the Research and Development Expansion Credit, which lead the two intermediate bases that do not measure recovery, and reject the Advanced Manufacturing Retooling Credit, which leads the scoring basis that is right in shape and is measured off a record that cannot see money coming back. ---

steps: Reproduced the published Watch from the monthly claims series. The index is the month's claims less the mean of the preceding twelve, over the square root of that mean, and it ties to the digit. ARD-2379 leads on 24.61 against 9.98 for the next cell, and the seventh cell in the state scores 2.53, so the six listed cells are the candidate set and the list is not marginal. **A desk that stops here places the team on Ardenmoor heavy civil.**

Checked that leader against its own history. The cell has scored between 21.17 and 25.52 in every October since 2019, because it does the bulk of its separating when the outdoor season closes, and against its own Octobers it is at 409 claims against a mean of 390. There is no event there.
Moved to a same-month reference over the trailing three years. THB-3363 now leads at 342 per cent. **A desk that stops here places the team on Thistlebrook motor vehicle parts.**

Read the work-sharing register against that comparison. STC-2023-006 ran at the cell's dominant employer from 04/2023 to 02/2026, which is exactly the three Octobers the comparison uses, and a short-time plan reduces hours rather than separating people. Against its full history the cell is at 84 claims against an October mean of 61.1, so it has returned to normal rather than deteriorated.

Extended the reference to the full history in claim counts. VEL-4931 now leads at 181 claims over its October average, the largest rise anywhere in the state. **A desk that stops here places the team on Vellinge Port warehousing.**

Normalised by covered employment. Four fulfilment registrations and one upward amendment took that cell from 9,951 covered in October 2025 to 27,081 now, and its rate moved from an October average of 10.17 per thousand to 10.34. More people are covered so more people claim, and the rate did not move. On the normalised basis MAR-2382 leads at 19.44 per thousand. **A desk that stops here places the team on Marchwood building equipment contractors, which is what the field coordinator argues for.**

Took the band of ordinary variation off the rest of the network. Across the eighty-four cells not on the list the largest movement in either direction is 2.98 sigma, and three watch-listed cells clear it while three do not, so the field is ARD-3116, HLC-5613 and MAR-2382.

Back-tested the seventeen filed session rosters against every basis the folder supports, fitting one coefficient through the origin on each. Claims sitting in same-employer same-separation-date actions reproduce all seventeen within 7.3 per cent at a coefficient of 0.5365, while all initial claims miss by 131 per cent, excess claims by 296 per cent, covered employment by 185 per cent and the Watch index itself by 328 per cent. The two sessions run in the same cell settle it: DEP-2024-06 and DEP-2025-03 are 82 claims against 80, excess 61 against 60 and index 14.20 against 11.11, yet one convened 33 workers and the other 6, and the only thing separating them is that 62 of the first cell's claims sat in actions against 12 of the second's.

ARD-3116 is barred in any case by protocol 2.4, since DEP-2026-09 was authorised on 2026-09-14 and ran on 2026-09-24 and its October claims carry separation dates of 2026-07-28 and 2026-08-04, which is the same action still filing on notice pay.

Placed the deployment at HLC-5613, which leads the nearest eligible cell by 9.48 times and leads the barred cell by 2.53 times even if the bar is ignored, and expects to convene 137 workers across the cycle's sessions.

steps: **Intake and clean the entry book.** Keep the operative version of each entry reference, drop cancelled entries, normalise the mixed KG and MT unit of measure, drop the two rows loaded twice, map tariff line to form group and keep scheduled forms only. The extract carries 648 references with a second version, 156 cancelled references and two exact duplicates.

**Read the Order before the papers.** Part 4.3 assesses a filing on the additional levy the release is expected to raise in the placement year, and the levy schedule puts the levy on net product weight of scheduled forms at a uniform rate. That disposes of the market development scorecard, which ranks on free-on-board value and puts Tessura first, and it disposes of any ranking on the existing book, which is a retrospective total rather than an increment.

**Rebuild MY2026 on the market that actually received the goods.** On declared destination the entrepot Ombrey tops the book at 82,036 tonnes. The onward consignment notices move 70,016 tonnes out of Ombrey to the markets that received it, and Halden becomes the true top of the book at 96,020. The partner statistics corroborate it independently, because they count only goods cleared for home use, so free-zone volume never appears in Ombrey's imports at all.

**Take the barrier inventory as the candidate set, not the answer.** Sirakut carries the largest restriction at 64,000 tonnes and Halden the second at 58,000, ahead of Norvale 30,500 and Corrasil 21,000. Refuse to rank on it until it is shown that a released tonne is a delivered tonne.

**Measure what the closed releases delivered.** The register states what was filed and what importers notified, not what arrived, so the outcome has to be computed from each destination administration's recorded arrivals, placement year against the year before effect. Seven of the forty-two sit in administrations reporting on a consignment basis, Halden and Andresk, where product moving through the free zone is booked to Ombrey, and those have to be corrected with the free-zone rows or the fit is wrong on exactly those cases.

**Find the ceiling.** Delivery does not scale with the volume released. KR-2019-06 and KR-2019-11 both released 18,000 tonnes into the MY2020 placement year with no preferential competitor in play and delivered 11,140 tonnes and 5,556 tonnes, 2.00 times apart, separated only by the 9,000 tonnes of listed split capacity Ulvarn had against Sirakut's 470,000. KR-2021-05 released 16,200 tonnes into a market with no listed establishment at all and delivered nothing.

**Find the preference term, and find that it is continuous.** A single rate on the ceiling leaves the residuals structured, and splitting them on a competitor yes-or-no flag does not fix it either, because within the group that carries a competitor the realisation runs from 0.043 to 0.535. Regressing realisation on the applied margin gives a slope of about 0.020 per point.

**Refuse to stop there, because that fit is not good.** Pooled over all forty-one measurable cases the single-slope fit has a residual standard deviation of 0.0725 on a quantity that only ranges from 0.04 to 0.62, and it misses a closed case by 515 per cent. The residuals are not noise, they are in two blocks, and the block a case falls in is its barrier type. Fit the two families separately and the residual standard deviation inside each falls to 0.0011, a factor of sixty-six, with the tariff family losing 0.01177 of realisation per point of margin and everything else losing 0.03290. The economics is ordinary: lifting a tariff-rate quota puts us back on the same duty footing as the rival so its preference only partly survives, while lifting a standard, a phytosanitary condition, a registration, a licence or a safeguard leaves the duty gap exactly where it was.

**Settle it on a pair nothing else can explain.** KR-2023-04 and KR-2025-22 are both releases into Kaltane, both on split product, both against a notified 14,000 tonnes, both facing the same 17.5 point Belkarn margin, and neither capped. They delivered 5,784 tonnes and 603 tonnes, 9.60 times apart. The only column that differs is the barrier type.

**Validate out of sample rather than in sample.** Fitted on the thirty releases in effect to 1 July 2023 and scored on the eleven later ones, the stratified specification is out by 0.54 per cent. The pooled single slope is out by 100.8 per cent, reading the margin on the in-force date by 133.8 per cent, dropping the ceiling by 85.6 per cent, and regressing on the notified offtake column by 27.6 per cent. That last one is worth naming, because `offtake_notified_t` on the register is what importers stated at the first annual review, twelve months after the release was already running, while the identically named field on the docket is what importers stated at a consultation round, so a model trained on one and scored on the other is being fed a different quantity and it lands on Sirakut.

**Apply the model to the docket, then the eligibility bar.** Halden leads on fillable volume at 58,000 tonnes, 2.76 times Corrasil, but its restriction is a technical standard and Belkarn has held 16.2 points of duty-free preference on split product into Halden since April 2021, so it converts at 0.0855 and is worth 4,957 tonnes. Sirakut is capped at 7,400 tonnes, so 88 per cent of its restriction could not be shipped by anyone we have listed, though its 9 point competitor costs it comparatively little because its instrument is a tariff quota. Part 4.4 forbids a dossier for a market with an open consultation proceeding, and `consultation_proceedings.csv` shows CP-2026-03 running past the window, which removes Norvale.

**Rank and commit.** Corrasil 12,992 tonnes, Vanthe 5,133, Halden 4,957, Ombrey 3,958, Sirakut 3,794, Tessura 1,754. File for Corrasil, by 2.53 times, worth 63,011 marks of additional levy at 4.85 marks per net tonne.

steps: Deduplicated the 2026 quote extract to the latest pull on each collection line and period, which removes 36 superseded rows in PHT alone, then rebuilt the field basis from the compilation manual and reproduced the published December 2026 levels for all eight shortlisted groups to within 0.05 index points.

Rebuilt the same field basis on the seven parallel runs and reproduced every filed field return in the conversion register to within 0.005 percentage points, which confirms the routine including the carry-forward on imputed lines and the January 2025 link at which the recorded adjustment factor entered compilation.

Constructed the feed basis as the collected variant's shelf price per unit of its own declared content, which is the obvious stand-in, and found it misses the filed divergences by up to 0.92 percentage points, so it is not what the feed measures.

Reconstructed the feed basis instead as the sales-weighted unit value per unit of net content over every pack size stocked in the stratum, and reproduced all seven filed feed returns to within 0.004 percentage points, which are SNK 4.95, BEV 4.65, AVE 1.96, BAK 4.81, ALC 3.69, CUT 2.75 and FRZ 4.29.

Split the gap into the content component, measurable from the field data, and a residual. The content component alone leaves between 0.17 and 1.31 percentage points unexplained on every run that has quantity-denominated packs, and the shortfall is one-directional, which is what a drift toward smaller packs does to a unit value.

Fitted the residual on the within-stratum quantity-discount gradient and got a coefficient of 3.42 with a worst residual of 0.111 percentage points. Fitted it instead on within-stratum content dispersion, the intuitive measure of how much room the mix has to move, and got a worst residual of 1.137 percentage points, ten times worse. BAK settles it: it carries the widest pack range of any run at 0.363 and the flattest gradient at 0.028, and its residual mix component is 0.17 percentage points, so room to move without a price gradient produces almost nothing.

Carried the fitted coefficient onto the eight shortlisted groups and weighted by relative importance. PHT 0.103 percentage points, PKG 0.064, MEA 0.046, HHC 0.036, PET 0.032, HAP 0.009, FRV 0.001, CLF 0.000.
Recommendation: the provision goes to PHT.

steps: Sized the slate the way anyone would on a first pass, quoted piece-price delta against the trailing twelve months of receipts net of the 55 reversals and with superseded part numbers rolled onto their ECO successors, and it leads with castings at $2,137,566.

Rebased volume onto BP-FY27-R3, the plan of record, since the bridge moves on what will be consumed rather than on what was received. On quoted terms the slate now leads with harnesses at $1,628,319 and castings drop to $1,302,600.

Rebuilt every quotation as a landed unit cost at the filed FY27 planning rate, adding chargeable-weight freight off the tendered rate card, duty by HTS code and origin net of preference, and packaging per carton, because the incumbents quote DDP into the consuming plant while the alternates quote FCA or EXW in three currencies. On that basis the slate leads with stampings at $1,033,832.

Stripped the volume Tarrant Ridge does not buy and price, reading the regime off the movement data rather than off the programme memo, since FIN-STD-12 clause 2 keeps consigned and customer-priced material out of the bridge. The slate now leads with seals at $809,591 while stampings collapse to $114,543.

Fixed the start of the qualification clock, which MCR-04 clause 4 dates the first Monday of the fiscal year the authorisation funds and FIN-STD-12 clause 1 makes the 2027 calendar year, so the clock starts 2027-01-04. Revision 7 took effect 2026-10-01 and the latest archived authorisation is 2026-09-16, so no project on file was dated under the clause.

Split the clock into the two processes it is made of. The base path to first shipment, measured on 17 of the 18 projects that need no customer approval, the one first article rejection left out because a rejection is an event inside a project rather than an attribute a candidate can be scored on, runs 100 days without new tooling and 224 with it, and the two sets of completions do not overlap at all. The source approval leg then sits on top of that.

Worked out what the source approval leg is a property of. Split by customer it is not estimable at either of the two customers the slate turns on, because Halloway holds three packages outstanding at 195, 293 and 772 days against two returned at 37 and 39, and Northmark holds five outstanding at 268 to 505 days against four returned at 35 to 37. Split instead on whether the alternate already holds released production on a part consumed on that customer's own programme, the corpus is absolute: ten packages of ten came back on an already released source, none slower than 45 days, while the 13 packages on a source that customer had never released have returned one in three years. The two populations are interleaved in time, with approvals granted in 2024, 2025 and 2026, so the best cut on the submission date still misplaces six of the 23 packages.

Scored the two readings on CR-2514, the one closed package that separates them. The population reading reproduces Finance's published line exactly and the returns reading misses it by 11 months and $64,332.

Phased each project into FY27 from the first whole month after the later of its forecast first shipment and the end of any committed volume window owed to the incumbent. MACH-2200 carries such a window to 2027-06-30, so it accrues from July, and the slate leads with MACH-2200 at $301,986 against HARN-5500 at $189,849.
Recommendation: Finance books $301,986.

steps: Divided presentations and attendances by the expected completeness for their report lag before computing anything else, as annex A.3 requires. The three most recent report days are 92, 97 and 99 per cent complete, and they sit inside the seven days every level is measured on.

Reproduced the detector from the dashboard's method sheet: 84 monitored series, 588 daily exceedance tests across ISO week 13, and the same fifteen open signals and the same scores the dashboard publishes. It puts SIG-2027-0247 at Meridian North first, at a score of 24.94.

Refused the ranked list. Meridian North took 85 per cent of the Calder Street caseload from 22 March and its attendance nearly doubled, which is why five of the fifteen open signals are Meridian North series. Assessed on the syndrome's share of attendances, which protocol 3.2 requires for a series hit by a service change, its acute respiratory excess is 9.8 presentations at q = 6.6e-01.

Refused the seasonal one. On the share footing the top scorer is SIG-2027-0253, conjunctivitis at Tarnwick, at 21.49. The spring term ended on 26 March and the same rise appears in the same fortnight in every year of the record, so against a baseline carrying a term-end indicator its excess is 37.6 at q = 0.24.

Refused the largest thing measured. SIG-2027-0246 at Port Hallow carries 360.4 excess presentations, was cohorted from 21 March, had no onsets after 25 March and was closed on the 27th, and its last seven days sit at z = -2.19. Nothing is in force there, so its expected yield over the fortnight is zero.

Read annex A.7, which says the annex measures what has already been observed and supplies no estimator for any future period, against protocol 2.5, which does not leave the choice open: a basis is scored on the returns where an elevation was in force at the panel that directed them, it may carry no coefficient fitted to those returns, and it reproduces them only at a mean absolute error below 45 presentations with no return missed by more than 130. The projection arithmetic is therefore tested rather than assumed. Attendance on a field day that has not happened yet is taken as the facility's four-week mean, which ten analysts out of ten would do here because the window is exactly two whole weeks and so is balanced across days of the week, and the sweep in step 9 shows the 7-, 14-, 28- and 56-day means all returning the same call.

Ran the test. Eight of the twenty-three returns had nothing in force at their own panel and returned nothing, so 2.5 excludes them and the fifteen in-force returns are where the bases separate. Seventeen candidate bases were scored. Four carry a coefficient fitted to the returns and 2.5 excludes them outright. Of the thirteen that remain, exactly two clear the bar, at 31.6 and 31.8, and they are the one proportional basis written two ways, continuously and day by day. Both name Dunmore Bay. The nearest failure is the level carried flat across the days the exposure survives, at 61.0 against the 45 allowed and a worst miss of 175.4 against 130, and every other flat, capped, shrunk and half-window basis fails with it.

Established what the failing bases get wrong, on the returns themselves. Five returns lost their exposure part way through the field window to an intervention already filed at their own panel, and on those a whole-window projection overshoots by 117 presentations on average against 16 for the adopted basis. Five ran their fortnight through a school term boundary at a series whose catchment moves on it, and on those a flat projection understates by 119.

Applied it. Saltcombe runs hardest at 15.22 a day but pays out for five days and returns 72.7. Kelby Vale carries 12.26 a day with nothing filed against it and leads every flat projection at 171.6, but its own expected count across the field window runs at 0.94 of the week its level was measured on, so it returns 161.3. Dunmore Bay carries the smallest level of the three at 9.17 a day and the largest expected path at 2.18, and returns 279.7, a factor of 1.73 over Kelby Vale. ---

steps: Built the burden ratio on the dictionary's definition, monthly housing cost over a twelfth of gross annual income, computed only where income is positive, which puts 41 of the 3,412 interviewed households outside the burden universe and leaves 3,371 in it.

Reproduced the Meridian Verge deliverable from its own published cut points, 0.27091, 0.44683 and 0.75505, and got its filed segment counts of 2,589, 3,653, 1,304 and 254 back exactly across 7,800 person records, so there is no data quality reason to distrust it. Its Method notes tab states its basis: one row per person record, unweighted.

Read section 3 of the standard, which puts the estimate on renter households in the region, weighted, each household counting once, and recomputed on that basis. The headline moves to 55.2 per cent above the reporting line rather than the 58.2 per cent records as collected give.

Tested the thirty per cent line. The weighted median burden is 0.3154, so the line cuts 0.0154 from the median, and shifting it by a hundredth either way reshuffles 6.6 points of households, by two and a half hundredths 16.0 points. It is a reporting threshold under clause 4.1 and not a boundary the data draws.

Searched the burden axis for any boundary at all, with a weighted kernel density on log burden across four bandwidths and all four estimation bases, and got one mode every time. Two, three and four component Gaussian mixtures on log burden agree with the eventual partition at adjusted Rand values of minus 0.041, minus 0.038 and minus 0.008, which is nil.

Read clause 4.3, which asks what the amount payable answers to rather than what the arrangement is called. Grouping on the arrangement columns gives either two populations, income indexed at 15.4 per cent against everything else at 84.6, or three, market set at 73.6, income share at 15.4 and site only at 11.0. Both are descriptions of the codes and neither is a test, so I went to the only records that observe a household twice.

Ran the test on the 140 re-contacted households. The ratio of amount to income held for every schedule household, worst drift 0.0021, and drifted for every other household, smallest 0.0756. That is one population and it is an absolute split with no threshold in it.

Looked at the 36 households whose size changed rather than only at income. Thirteen of them had the amount step by exactly 52 dollars per person, the other 23 did not move at all, and none of the thirteen was a schedule household. Six schedule households changed size and their amount followed their income instead, which is what tells the two responses apart.

Recovered the membership, since no file records the fee. Fitting monthly rent on persons in the household within each site community separates the 32 communities completely: 17 sit at a slope of 42.4 to 59.7 with R squared 0.853 to 0.962, and the remaining 15 return slopes between minus 272.3 and 217.0 with R squared never above 0.163. Every site community carries at least 7 sampled households, so no household is left unassignable.

Built the distribution table within the three. Medians 0.3306, 0.3045 and 0.3063, interquartile ranges 0.0653, 0.2554 and 0.2269, ninetieth percentiles 0.4133, 0.6699 and 0.6047, and severe burden 2.7, 18.1 and 17.8 per cent.

Tested the divisions the file still invites and refused each one. The 28, 30 and 32 per cent covered bands inside the first population differ in median burden, 0.3197, 0.3282 and 0.3531, and are one arrangement applied at three rates, which 4.3 reports within a population. The 44 master metered site households sit in nine block groups, and metering routes the utility bill rather than changing what the household pays. Assistance enrolment is refused by the extract's own note that enrolment does not establish how the payable amount is set.

Put the three against the design. The severe burden gap between the third population and the first is 15.14 points against a delete a group jackknife standard error of 1.76 on the 80 shipped replicates, which is 8.6 standard errors.
Recommendation: adopt three populations, at 15.4, 5.1 and 79.6 per cent.

One thing the provision turns on is stated nowhere: which adjustment year an endorsement falls in.

**Recover the December convention.** The index ends at November 2026. `provisional_determination_register.csv` carries the 42 values the desk filed for AY2021 to AY2026; of five candidate rules the mean of the three most recent published prints reproduces 41 and the best rival reproduces

3. **Compute the AY2027 factors.** Steel leads at 1.1240 because its move landed at the end of 2025 and carried into the 2026 average in full; copper is only 1.1020 because its surge came too late in 2026 to move that year's average.

Attributing each work order to the year its endorsement is dated reproduces all 1253 to the cent, including every one of the 393 that carries money; attributing it to the year its schedule was filed for reproduces 1086, failing on 167 lines and missing by up to 280%.
